title: MLB trade deadline 2026 top storylines, bold predictions and best available players
content:
Happy Trade Deadline Week, as the clock goes tick tock, tick tock…

Discussions are heating up, with all 30 clubs exchanging texts, emails and phone calls at a fast and furious pace. Some blockbuster deals are expected, and there are bound to be a few surprises, so get ready for the fireworks show, which will end officially at 6 p.m. ET on Aug. 3.

There has been very little action thus far, with the biggest deal of note the swap between the Boston Red Sox and Washington Nationals that sent Curtis Mead to Boston and Connelly Early to Washington. Unfortunately, the impact of that deal was put on hold when Mead suffered a fractured wrist during his second at-bat in his Boston debut. Early, who was on the injured list at the time of the deal, is expected to be out a couple more weeks with elbow inflammation. Eventually, that trade should help both teams. (The Texas Rangers and Los Angeles Angels pulled off a smaller deal on Wednesday, with the Rangers acquiring catcher Logan O’Hoppe and reliever Chase Silseth for infield prospect Angel Arredondo.)

The Mead-Early trade could be a sign of things to come, as it was between two teams with a shot at a postseason spot rather than a trade between a true buyer and a true seller. We could see several of those types of deals, as only a handful of teams are further than five games out from at least a wild-card berth.

That deal also shows that teams will have to overpay for right-handed power. Putting aside Mead’s injury (which was just bad luck), when evaluating the trade, the Nationals got the better end of the deal in terms of value, but both teams got exactly what they needed. Front offices aren’t looking to “win” trades but rather to put their team in a better position to win a championship. The Red Sox likely didn’t “win” this deal in terms of future value, but before Mead’s unfortunate injury, it put them in a much better position to win this year. This could be a sign of things to come in future deals at this year’s deadline.

In talking with front-office heads in both leagues, I’m hearing that teams are not expecting a flurry of moves until the weekend. According to the execs I’ve spoken with, several teams are still deciding not only whether to buy or sell, but also what they are looking for to improve. For several teams, their needs are different than they were even a week ago. That indecision has made deals more difficult to close so far.

With all of that in mind, here are the things you need to keep track of as we head into the heart of trade deadline mania.

First, let’s look at the buyers, sellers and everyone in between:

American League: Rays, Yankees, Red Sox, White Sox, Guardians, Rangers, Mariners and Astros

National League: Dodgers, Brewers, Braves, Phillies and Cubs

American League: Angels, Royals, Athletics and Blue Jays

National League: Mets, Giants and Rockies

American League: Orioles and Twins

National League: Pirates, Cardinals, Padres and Diamondbacks

American League: Tigers

National League: Marlins, Reds and Nationals

The headliner of this year’s deadline is two-time AL Cy Young Award winner Skubal. But will the Tigers actually trade him? If they do, they’ll likely also trade their second-best starting pitcher, Casey Mize, and their closer, Kenley Jansen.

It really could go either way. They are still within arm’s reach of the wild-card but aren’t playing well at the moment. However, through Tuesday’s games, they were tied with the Rays in run differential (+39), reflecting the talent on their roster. If they trade Skubal and/or Mize, their season is basically over.

That said, since they haven’t been able to extend Skubal and aren’t even negotiating a new deal right now, I believe they would be better off trading him and getting back a haul of prospects who will make them better in the long term. They have a strong core of young players, including the best catcher in baseball in Dillon Dingler, one of the best young hitters in the game in rookie Kevin McGonigle and an emerging superstar in left fielder Riley Greene.

If there are trades available that allow them to load up on pitching at both the major- and minor-league levels in deals for Skubal and Mize, then that’s the direction they should go. I don’t think the Tigers are a World Series team this year despite the parity in the AL.

I do understand the argument for going for it because there isn’t a dominant team in the AL, but if the Tigers keep Skubal and Mize and don’t make the playoffs, they’ll have set the organization back a few years.

The Mets are expected to be the most aggressive and most prolific sellers, as they have two starting pitchers to dangle in Freddy Peralta and Clay Holmes and a plethora of bullpen arms, including Luke Weaver, A.J. Minter, Brooks Raley and Huascar Brazobán. They also have right-handed hitting outfielders Luis Robert Jr. and Tyrone Taylor and a couple of catchers everyone wants in Francisco Alvarez and Luis Torrens.

Meanwhile, the Yankees could be the biggest buyers with their needs growing rapidly due to injuries. The latest blow came when star left fielder Cody Bellinger was placed on the IL with a hamstring injury. He will be out four to six weeks, which means they might not get Aaron Judge or Bellinger back until September or later.

The Yankees have a lot of needs, from a right-handed hitting outfielder to a right-handed hitting catcher to a starting pitcher to a high-leverage reliever. They’ll also be in play if any impact players are actually traded, like Skubal and Padres closer Mason Miller. The Yankees have plenty to offer in trades thanks to a deep farm system, multiple major-league starters they could include in deals, as well as left-handed hitting outfielders already in The Show.

New York, New York … Frank Sinatra and Jay Z, get ready to sing, baby.

There just aren’t a lot of sellers, and most of them don’t have a lot to sell. The Rockies could deal their star catcher Hunter Goodman, but beyond that, they only have back-of-the-rotation and bullpen arms to deal. The Royals could dangle starting pitchers Michael Wacha and Seth Lugo along with Lane Thomas — who is more of a fourth-outfielder type — or a set-up reliever, but not much beyond that. The A’s are likely to hold on to their young core, leaving back-end starters and role players as their only major trade chips.

Among the other sellers, the Angels have Reid Detmers, José Soriano, Zach Neto and Jo Adell to offer. The Giants and Blue Jays have some solid veterans on expiring contracts available: Robbie Ray, Tyler Mahle and Luis Arraez in San Francisco and Kevin Gausman, Shane Bieber, Daulton Varsho and George Springer in Toronto. Aside from those teams and the Mets, most of the teams making deals will be contenders.

A few weeks ago, all we kept hearing was how Mike Trout was going to be traded to the Phillies. Well, we can stop the rumors; it’s not happening. He doesn’t want to be traded, he has a full no-trade clause, Angels owner Arte Moreno doesn’t want to trade him and the Angels interim GM John Mozeliak says he’s not going to trade him.

Similarly, Mason Miller isn’t going anywhere. Teams may offer the Padres their best prospect, and the answer will still be no. The only way he is traded is if it’s a Juan Soto-type deal where the Padres get four top-10 prospects in return. As of this writing, no one has made an offer close to that.

For much of the season, it was rumored that the Twins would be open to trading stars Joe Ryan and Byron Buxton, but that isn’t happening. In fact, the Twins are looking to add and are trying to improve their bullpen.

The Marlins’ season took a turn recently with a 12-game losing streak, but even that isn’t likely to push them to trade Sandy Alcantara. And the Giants aren’t trading Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman at this trade deadline. Their bad contracts and current underperformance complicate any potential deals. Of course, I learned a long time ago in baseball that anything can happen, but as of now there is zero momentum.

If the Dodgers win their third consecutive title this year with a payroll that is $300 million more than that of the Brewers and Rays, it will just fuel MLB owners who want to impose a lockout for the entire 2027 season in order to get a hard salary cap like in the NFL, NBA and NHL. However, if there is a World Series between the Brewers and Rays and one of them acquires Skubal at the deadline and the other team also adds big, then the argument for the cap should lessen during these labor negotiations and open a clearer path to an agreement in time for a 2027 season.

The MLBPA should be rooting hard for those small-market teams to outmaneuver the big-market teams at the deadline.

David Stearns, New York Mets

Yes, he’s under contract for two more years, but in all probability has one more year to turn things around and keep his job long-term. He has the most talent to trade at the deadline, and he also will be under the most pressure.

Brian Cashman, New York Yankees

As the Yankees GM, he’s always dealing with the most pressure, but unlike Stearns, Cashman isn’t fighting to keep his job but rather to get the Yankees back to the World Series.

Jerry Dipoto, Seattle Mariners

The Mariners are the most disappointing team in baseball. Based on their present roster, they should be in first place with a healthy lead, but instead are fighting for their survival. Seattle needs to trade for a right-handed impact bat and another high-leverage reliever if they’re going to win the AL West. The pressure is on while this team’s window for winning is still open.

Dave Dombrowski, Philadelphia Phillies

The Phillies are an aging team with a roster filled with stars and scrubs. When the trio of Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo start, they are a playoff team. When anyone else starts, they are one of the worst teams in baseball.

Their offense is centered around Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, Trea Turner and Brandon Marsh, but after that they don’t have a major-league-average performer this year and Turner has really struggled. They are built to win in October but might not get there if Dombrowski doesn’t deal for a back-end starter (or two), another reliever and a right-handed hitting outfielder.

The pressure is on with the Phillies’ contention window closing rapidly.

Chris Getz, Chicago White Sox

Getz has taken Chicago from 102 losses last year to first place in the AL Central. If he’s going to hold on to the division lead, he needs to trade for a starting pitcher, a reliever and a catcher. The White Sox are the best story in baseball, and now it’s time to finish the job.

Dana Brown, Houston Astros

Brown is working under an expiring contract. With most of his offseason moves to improve their pitching backfiring, he might need a strong trade at the deadline and a playoff berth to get what would be a well-deserved contract extension.

Andrew Friedman, Los Angeles Dodgers

Easily the least pressure in baseball. Friedman’s organization has the most money, the best front office and the best talent top to bottom. He doesn’t have to make a single trade for his team to be the favorite to win it all once again.

Matt Arnold, Milwaukee Brewers

Arnold has the second-best team in the sport despite having one of the smallest payrolls. His farm system is loaded. Even if he does nothing, the Brewers are very likely to win the NL Central. He’ll try to make an impact and take a shot at acquiring another playoff starter, but there is no pressure if he doesn’t land one.

If there is going to be a surprise at this year’s deadline, it’s going to come from a small- to middle-market team that hasn’t been able to sign their young star players to long-term contracts deciding they want to trade them now while their trade value is at its peak.

Examples of this could be CJ Abrams of the Nationals, Elly De La Cruz of the Reds, Oneil Cruz of the Pirates or Adley Rutschman of the Orioles.
